vignette:
At 69, Minh has spent most of his adult life working as a plumber, moving through basements, utility rooms, apartment corridors, and strangers’ homes with the practiced ease of someone used to entering tight spaces and solving practical problems. He is married and has lived in the United States for many years, but when he speaks about the period that still grips him, his mind returns to a time of captivity that he cannot recount in a straight line. He says he knows exactly what happened, yet when he tries to tell it, the words disappear. He starts somewhere in the middle, stops, looks down, presses his fingers into the side of his neck, and says that once the images begin, it is “like a film” playing again in front of him. He does not describe the whole event in sequence so much as relive pieces of it: being confined with men he did not trust, watching their bodies shift in a cramped space, tracking their movements because any sudden turn or step toward him might mean danger. What remains most vivid is the feeling of being trapped with male captors and having no safe way out.

In the years after, the memories did not settle into the past. They returned with a force that felt bodily as much as mental. If he was alone with a man, especially in an enclosed place, his body reacted before he could think. He would feel a wave of nausea rise abruptly, or a familiar pain seize in his neck, and in that moment he was no longer simply in a customer’s basement or a back utility room for a repair. He was back in the atmosphere of captivity, braced and scanning. He describes strong physical reactions when reminded of what happened, as though his body recognizes the danger before he can name it. Sudden movements by other people put him immediately on guard. If a male customer stepped quickly behind him while he was crouched under a sink, Minh’s whole body would tighten and he would jerk upright, heart pounding, ashamed afterward but unable to tell himself it was nothing.

Over time he began organizing his life around getting through these moments. Before entering any building, he checks where the exits are and how quickly he could leave if he had to. This is so automatic now that he often does it without comment: in apartment complexes, restaurants, medical offices, even at family gatherings. As a plumber, he prefers jobs where doors stay open and where someone else is nearby, and he has become reluctant to take work that would leave him alone with a male client in a closed room. He does not announce this openly; instead he finds reasons to reschedule, asks another worker to come along, or hurries through jobs while keeping himself positioned near a doorway. At home, where his wife expects him to feel most at ease, he remains watchful. He notices footsteps, shifts in posture, the angle of a person entering a room. Even inside his own house he does not fully let down his guard.

He has also developed quieter ways of managing what comes up inside him. When the memories start, he tries to detach from them, as if stepping away internally might keep him from being swallowed by the images. He avoids dates and anniversaries connected to the period of captivity because he has learned that those days pull the memories closer. He does not always tell his wife why he becomes withdrawn at certain times of year; she mainly sees that he grows tense, less talkative, more difficult to reach. The consequence has been a narrowing of his life. Practical jobs still get done, bills are paid, and the outward structure of his days remains intact, but much of his energy goes into anticipating where he might feel trapped, who might trigger that old alarm, and how he would get out.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was not a single new event so much as the accumulation of these moments and his growing awareness that age has not loosened their hold. Recently, during a plumbing call, he found himself alone with a male customer in a narrow laundry room. When the man turned suddenly toward him to ask a question, Minh felt nausea surge and his neck lock with pain. He had to steady himself against the wall and could barely finish the job. Trying later to explain to his wife why he was so shaken, he again lost the thread and could not find the words, which left him frustrated and defeated. He comes to treatment frightened by how quickly his body still reacts and by how little control he feels he has when the film of memory begins to play. At the same time, he hopes that if he can finally speak about what happened without losing himself in it, he might move through his work, his home, and even a room with other men without always needing to know the fastest way out.
